lesson.title: Explanation
lesson.summary: Demonstrates Java's tricky interaction between inheritance, field hiding, polymorphic dispatch, and constructor initialization order. A B object is created through an A-typed reference, and the output reveals how fields are accessed based on declared type vs. actual type, and how calling overridable methods from constructors can see uninitialized subclass fields.
steps: new B() is invoked. Java starts B's constructor: B() { super(); show(); n += 100; }. The first statement is super(), so control transfers to A's constructor.
A's field initializers run before A's constructor body: s = "A", n = 1. B's field initializers have NOT run yet, so B's s is null and B's n is 0 (default values for String and int).

A's constructor body executes: show() is called. Because show() is not static or final, Java uses dynamic dispatch on the actual object (a B instance), so B.show() runs. B.show() evaluates: s (B's field, still null) + n (B's field, still 0) + super.s (A's field, "A") + super.n (A's field, 1) + " ". String concatenation: null + 0 becomes "null0", + "A" becomes "null0A", + 1 becomes "null0A1", + " " becomes "null0A1 ". This is printed.
Back in A's constructor body after show() returns: n += 10. This modifies A's n field: 1 + 10 = 11. A's constructor finishes.
Control returns to B's constructor. Now B's own field initializers run in source order: s = "B", n = 2. Then the instance initializer block executes: n *= 3, so n = 2 * 3 = 6.

B's constructor body continues: show() is called again. Dynamic dispatch selects B.show(). Now all fields are properly initialized: s = "B", n = 6, super.s = "A", super.n = 11. Output: "B" + 6 + "A" + 11 + " " = "B6A11 ". This is printed.
B's constructor body finishes: n += 100. B's n field: 6 + 100 = 106. The object is now fully constructed. x references this B object (with declared type A).

x.show() is called in main. Dynamic dispatch sees the actual object is a B, so B.show() runs. Current values: s = "B", n = 106, super.s = "A", super.n = 11. Output: "B" + 106 + "A" + 11 + " " = "B106A11 ". This is printed.

System.out.println(...) evaluates its argument left to right: x.s is A's s field ("A") because x's declared type is A. x.n is A's n field (11). ((B) x).s is B's s field ("B") because the cast changes the compile-time type to B. ((B) x).n is B's n field (106). x.who() is a static call on type A, so it calls A.who() which returns "a". ((A) null).who() is also a static call on type A, so it calls A.who() which returns "a" (no NullPointerException because static calls don't dereference). All concatenated: "A" + 11 + "B" + 106 + "a" + "a" = "A11B106aa". println prints this string followed by a newline.
connections: B extends A, so B inherits A's fields (s, n) and methods (show, who), but B also declares its own s and n which hide A's copies.
B's constructor calls super() which triggers A's constructor. A's constructor calls show(), which is a virtual call that dispatches to B's show() because the object is a B.
In main, x is declared as type A but holds a B object. x.show() uses the actual object type (B) for dispatch, while x.s and x.n use the declared type (A) to pick which field to access.
x.who() and ((A) null).who() both use static dispatch based on the expression type A, so both call A.who() regardless of the actual object or nullness.
The cast ((B) x) changes the compile-time type to B, allowing access to B's hidden fields s and n.
pitfalls: Calling an overridable method (show) from a constructor is dangerous: during super() the subclass fields are still at their default values (null, 0), so the output 'null0A1' reflects uninitialized state that would never occur in normal use.
x.s and x.n access A's fields (the declared type), NOT B's fields, even though x holds a B object. You need a cast to B to reach B's hidden fields.
x.who() calls A.who() because who is static and dispatch is based on the reference type A, not the actual object type B. This is different from how show() dispatches.
((A) null).who() does NOT throw a NullPointerException because static method calls do not dereference the reference. The null is irrelevant.
B's instance initializer block { n *= 3; } runs after field initializers but before the constructor body, so n goes 2 → 6 before show() is called in B's constructor.
The super.n in B.show() refers to A's n field (value 11 after the constructor), not B's n field (value 6). They are completely separate storage locations.

output.explanation: The program prints one line: 'null0A1 B6A11 bA' followed by a newline. The first part comes from the constructor-time show() call (when B's fields are still at defaults), the second from the explicit x.show() call (when all fields are fully initialized), and the rest from the println expression evaluating each sub-expression left to right.

concepts.explanation: When you call a method on an object, Java looks at the actual type of the object (not the variable's declared type) to decide which version to run. So calling show() on an A-typed variable that holds a B object runs B's show().
A subclass declares a field with the same name as a superclass field. Both fields still exist; the type of the expression decides which one a field access names.

When a subclass constructor calls super(), the superclass constructor runs first. If that constructor calls a method that the subclass overrides, the subclass version runs even though the subclass's own fields haven't been set up yet.

Static methods belong to the class name, not to any object. Java picks which version to run based on the type written on the left side of the dot, not the object's actual type. A null reference is fine because no object is actually used.
Before a constructor body runs, all field initializers (like int n = 2) and instance initializer blocks (like { n *= 3; }) run in the order they appear in the source code.

lesson.title: Explanation
lesson.summary: Demonstrates how Java's initialization order, field hiding, dynamic dispatch for instance methods, and static resolution for static methods interact when a subclass object is created and accessed through a superclass reference.
steps: new B() is called. Memory is allocated for a B object. All fields are set to their Java defaults: A.s=null, A.n=0, B.s=null, B.n=0. Since B extends A, the superclass A must be initialized first.
A's fields are initialized in source order: A.s = "A", A.n = 1. B's fields are still null/0 at this point.
A has no instance initializer blocks, so we go straight to A's constructor body: show() is called, then n += 10.

show() is called on this (which is a B object at runtime). Because show() is overridden in B, dynamic dispatch calls B.show(). B.show() prints s + n + super.s + super.n + " ". At this moment, B's fields have NOT been initialized yet, so B.s = null and B.n = 0. A's fields are already set: super.s = "A", super.n = 1. The expression evaluates as: null + 0 + "A" + 1 + " " = "null0A1 ".
Back in A's constructor body, after show() returns: n += 10. This is A's n field (the one A's constructor is working on). A.n was 1, now A.n = 11. B.n is still 0.
A's constructor finishes. Now B's own initialization begins. B's fields are set in source order: B.s = "B", B.n = 2.
B's instance initializer block runs: { n *= 3; }. This refers to B's own n field (the nearest one in scope). B.n was 2, now B.n = 6.

B's constructor body runs. The first statement super() already completed (that's how we got here). Next: show() is called. Again, dynamic dispatch calls B.show(). Now B's fields ARE initialized: B.s = "B", B.n = 6. A's fields: super.s = "A", super.n = 11. The expression: "B" + 6 + "A" + 11 + " " = "B6A11 ".
Back in B's constructor body: n += 100. This is B's n field. B.n was 6, now B.n = 106. The constructor finishes and the fully built B object is assigned to x.

Now in main: x.show() is called. x is declared as type A but holds a B object. show() is an instance method, so dynamic dispatch uses the runtime type (B). B.show() prints: s + n + super.s + super.n + " ". B.s = "B", B.n = 106, super.s = "A", super.n = 11. Result: "B106A11 ".

System.out.println evaluates the full expression left to right. x.s: x is declared as type A, so this accesses A's s field = "A". x.n: A's n field = 11. ((B) x).s: the cast changes the compile-time type to B, so this accesses B's s field = "B". ((B) x).n: B's n field = 106.

Continuing the expression: x.who() — who() is a static method. Static methods resolve by the compile-time type of the reference, which is A. So A.who() is called, returning "a". This does NOT use the runtime type.

Continuing: ((A) null).who() — who() is static, so the object reference is never dereferenced. The null is irrelevant. The compile-time type is A, so A.who() is called, returning "a". No NullPointerException is thrown.
All pieces are concatenated: "A" + 11 + "B" + 106 + "a" + "a" = "A11B106aa". println prints this string followed by a newline.
connections: B extends A, so B inherits A's fields (s, n) and methods (show, who). B re-declares s and n, which hides A's copies. B overrides show() and who().

The constructor chain is: new B() → B() body starts → super() → A() body → A's show() call → B.show() (dynamic dispatch) → returns → A's n += 10 → back in B() → B's fields set → B's initializer → B's show() call → B's n += 100.

In main, x is declared as type A but holds a B object. This means: instance methods use B's version (dynamic dispatch), instance fields use A's hidden copy (compile-time type), and static methods use A's version (static resolution).
pitfalls: Calling an overridden method from a superclass constructor is a classic bug source. The subclass fields are still at their defaults (null/0) when the method runs, giving unexpected results like 'null' in the output.
x.s gives A's field (value 1 for n, "A" for s) because x is declared as type A, even though the object is a B. You must cast to B to see B's fields.
x.who() calls A.who() (returns "a") because static methods resolve by the declared type, not the runtime type. This is different from instance methods which use the runtime type.
((A) null).who() does NOT throw a NullPointerException because who() is static. The null reference is never actually used to access an object.
The instance initializer block { n *= 3; } in B runs AFTER B's field declarations but BEFORE B's constructor body. This is why n becomes 6 before the += 100 in the constructor.

output.explanation: The first line prints 'null0A1 B2A1 ' from the two show() calls during construction. The second line prints 'A11B2bba' from the println in main. Together the full output is: 'null0A1 B2A1 A11B2bba'.

concepts.explanation: When you call a method that is overridden, Java looks at the actual object's class (the runtime type) to decide which version to run, not the variable's declared type.
A subclass declares a field with the same name as a superclass field. Both fields still exist; the type of the expression decides which one a field access names.
When you call a static method, Java looks at the type written before the dot (the compile-time type) to decide which version to run. It does NOT look at the runtime object.

Inside a constructor, the object is being built step by step. If an overridden method is called before the subclass's fields are set, those fields still hold their default values (null for objects, 0 for numbers).
A cast like (B) x changes which fields and methods the compiler allows you to use, but the actual object in memory is unchanged.
Static methods belong to the class, not to any object. You can call them through a null reference without crashing because no object is needed.

reviewedLesson.title: Explanation
reviewedLesson.summary: Demonstrates how Java's initialization order, field hiding, dynamic dispatch for instance methods, and static resolution for static methods interact when a subclass object is created and accessed through a superclass reference.
steps: new B() is called. Memory is allocated for a B object. All fields are set to their Java defaults: A.s=null, A.n=0, B.s=null, B.n=0. Since B extends A, the superclass A must be initialized first.
A's fields are initialized in source order: A.s = "A", A.n = 1. B's fields are still null/0 at this point.
A has no instance initializer blocks, so we go straight to A's constructor body: show() is called, then n += 10.

show() is called on this (which is a B object at runtime). Because show() is overridden in B, dynamic dispatch calls B.show(). B.show() prints s + n + super.s + super.n + " ". At this moment, B's fields have NOT been initialized yet, so B.s = null and B.n = 0. A's fields are already set: super.s = "A", super.n = 1. The expression evaluates as: null + 0 + "A" + 1 + " " = "null0A1 ".
Back in A's constructor body, after show() returns: n += 10. This is A's n field (the one A's constructor is working on). A.n was 1, now A.n = 11. B.n is still 0.
A's constructor finishes. Now B's own initialization begins. B's fields are set in source order: B.s = "B", B.n = 2.
B's instance initializer block runs: { n *= 3; }. This refers to B's own n field (the nearest one in scope). B.n was 2, now B.n = 6.

B's constructor body runs. The first statement super() already completed (that's how we got here). Next: show() is called. Again, dynamic dispatch calls B.show(). Now B's fields ARE initialized: B.s = "B", B.n = 6. A's fields: super.s = "A", super.n = 11. The expression: "B" + 6 + "A" + 11 + " " = "B6A11 ".
Back in B's constructor body: n += 100. This is B's n field. B.n was 6, now B.n = 106. The constructor finishes and the fully built B object is assigned to x.

Now in main: x.show() is called. x is declared as type A but holds a B object. show() is an instance method, so dynamic dispatch uses the runtime type (B). B.show() prints: s + n + super.s + super.n + " ". B.s = "B", B.n = 106, super.s = "A", super.n = 11. Result: "B106A11 ".

System.out.println evaluates the full expression left to right. x.s: x is declared as type A, so this accesses A's s field = "A". x.n: A's n field = 11. ((B) x).s: the cast changes the compile-time type to B, so this accesses B's s field = "B". ((B) x).n: B's n field = 106.

Continuing the expression: x.who() — who() is a static method. Static methods resolve by the compile-time type of the reference, which is A. So A.who() is called, returning "a". This does NOT use the runtime type.

Continuing: ((A) null).who() — who() is static, so the object reference is never dereferenced. The null is irrelevant. The compile-time type is A, so A.who() is called, returning "a". No NullPointerException is thrown.
All pieces are concatenated: "A" + 11 + "B" + 106 + "a" + "a" = "A11B106aa". println prints this string followed by a newline.
connections: B extends A, so B inherits A's fields (s, n) and methods (show, who). B re-declares s and n, which hides A's copies. B overrides show() and who().

The constructor chain is: new B() → B() body starts → super() → A() body → A's show() call → B.show() (dynamic dispatch) → returns → A's n += 10 → back in B() → B's fields set → B's initializer → B's show() call → B's n += 100.

In main, x is declared as type A but holds a B object. This means: instance methods use B's version (dynamic dispatch), instance fields use A's hidden copy (compile-time type), and static methods use A's version (static resolution).
A is declared as a static nested class. It is inside another class, but does not need an object of that enclosing class. Java distinguishes this from a non-static inner class.
B is declared as a static nested class. It is inside another class, but does not need an object of that enclosing class. Java distinguishes this from a non-static inner class.
B extends A: B is the subclass and A is its superclass. Nesting groups the classes in the source; inheritance connects their behavior. These are separate relationships.

With the standard java.lang.System, System.out is a java.io.PrintStream for text output. print writes its text; println also ends the line. These are standard-library tools, while classes declared in this selection are your own code.
pitfalls: Calling an overridden method from a superclass constructor is a classic bug source. The subclass fields are still at their defaults (null/0) when the method runs, giving unexpected results like 'null' in the output.
x.s gives A's field (value 1 for n, "A" for s) because x is declared as type A, even though the object is a B. You must cast to B to see B's fields.
x.who() calls A.who() (returns "a") because static methods resolve by the declared type, not the runtime type. This is different from instance methods which use the runtime type.
((A) null).who() does NOT throw a NullPointerException because who() is static. The null reference is never actually used to access an object.
The instance initializer block { n *= 3; } in B runs AFTER B's field declarations but BEFORE B's constructor body. This is why n becomes 6 before the += 100 in the constructor.

output.explanation: The first line prints 'null0A1 B2A1 ' from the two show() calls during construction. The second line prints 'A11B2bba' from the println in main. Together the full output is: 'null0A1 B2A1 A11B2bba'.

concepts.explanation: When you call a method that is overridden, Java looks at the actual object's class (the runtime type) to decide which version to run, not the variable's declared type.
A subclass declares a field with the same name as a superclass field. Both fields still exist; the type of the expression decides which one a field access names.
When you call a static method, Java looks at the type written before the dot (the compile-time type) to decide which version to run. It does NOT look at the runtime object.

Inside a constructor, the object is being built step by step. If an overridden method is called before the subclass's fields are set, those fields still hold their default values (null for objects, 0 for numbers).
A cast like (B) x changes which fields and methods the compiler allows you to use, but the actual object in memory is unchanged.
Static methods belong to the class, not to any object. You can call them through a null reference without crashing because no object is needed.
A class declared static inside another class. It does not need an instance of the enclosing class. It is nested, but is not a non-static inner class.

lesson.title: Explanation
lesson.summary: Polymorphism means that when you call an overridden instance method, Java picks the version based on the real class of the object, not the type of the variable holding it. In this code, x is declared as A but holds a B object, so `x.show()` runs B's version. However, fields and static methods do NOT work this way — they always follow the declared type of the variable or cast. So `x.s` gives A's field, but `x.show()` gives B's method. The cast `((B) x)` changes which fields you can see but doesn't change the object. A static call like `((A) null).who()` works fine because static methods don't need a real object; Java just uses the type in the parentheses to decide which version to call.
steps: When `x.show()` is called on line 19, Java looks at the real object (a B) and picks B's `show()`, even though x is declared as type A. This is polymorphism: the method that runs depends on what the object actually IS, not what the variable name says. B's `show()` prints `s + n + super.s + super.n + " "`, where `s` and `n` are B's own fields and `super.s` / `super.n` are A's fields, so it prints `B106A11 `. The key distinction: if you had written `x.s` (a field), Java would give you A's `s` ("A") because fields are NOT polymorphic — they follow the declared type. But `x.show()` IS polymorphic because it's an overridden instance method. This same rule caused a surprise during construction: inside A's constructor, `show()` was called while building a B object, so B's version ran even though B's fields hadn't been set yet, printing `null0A11 `. For static methods like `who()`, the declared type wins: `x.who()` calls A's version ("a") because x is typed A, and `((A) null).who()` also calls A's version ("a") because the cast says A — the null never matters since static methods don't need a real object. So the final println produces `A11B106aa`: fields and statics follow the declared type, only overridden instance methods follow the real object.

reviewedLesson.title: How polymorphism applies here
reviewedLesson.summary: The declaration says x has type A, while new B() creates a B object. The variable's declared type and the object's actual class are different pieces of information.
steps: For an overridden instance method called through x, Java uses the actual object's class. If B overrides that method, its version runs even though the variable is declared A. This choice at runtime is called dynamic dispatch, a form of polymorphism.

The same rule applies to an overridable method called inside a constructor. A superclass constructor can call into subclass code before the subclass's written field initializers run. The subclass's own fields may still hold default values such as null or 0. They do not turn into the superclass's fields. This is why construction order matters.

Fields follow a different rule. If A and B declare a field with the same name, both fields still exist. An access through x selects the A field because that is the variable's declared type. A cast to B can select the B field. The cast changes the type of that expression, not the object itself.

Static methods belong to classes. A static call through x selects using A, rather than asking the object which version to run. A subclass static method can hide a superclass method; it does not override it. A static call through a null reference does not itself dereference an object. Writing the class name directly makes the choice clearer.

@Override asks the compiler to check that a method really overrides or implements an eligible method. The annotation does not cause runtime dispatch, and an override can work without it. Constructors are not inherited or overridden; calls made inside them can still use overridden instance methods.

In an application, several kinds of screen item can share one base type but each draw itself differently. Calling the same instance method can reach each item's own version. Avoid calling such overridable methods from a constructor when the child may still be unfinished; use an appropriate private/final helper or a separate step after construction.

concepts.explanation: For an overridden instance method, Java chooses the version using the real class of the object at runtime. A variable typed A can hold a B object and call B's version. Fields and static methods follow different rules.
